# The Trapezium Rule: Error Term

## 0. The statement, and the hypothesis it needs

Throughout, $a<b$ are real numbers, $n$ is a positive integer,
$$h=\frac{b-a}{n},\qquad x_r=a+rh\quad(r=0,1,\dots,n),$$
and the *trapezium approximation* to $\int_a^b f$ associated with the normal subdivision
$P=\{x_0,x_1,\dots,x_n\}$ is
$$T_n \;:=\; \frac h2\Big(f(x_0)+f(x_n)+2\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}f(x_r)\Big).$$

### 0.1 Why "integrable" is not enough

As literally posed, the assertion is that for every $f$ integrable on $[a,b]$ the error of the
trapezium rule equals $\dfrac{(b-a)^3f''(\xi)}{12n^2}$ for some $\xi\in[a,b]$. This cannot be
correct, because an integrable function need not possess a second derivative at any point, so the
symbol $f''(\xi)$ need not denote anything. The failure is not merely notational; it occurs even
for functions that *are* twice differentiable at all but one point:

> **Counterexample.** Take $a=-1$, $b=1$, $f(x)=|x|$ and any **odd** $n$. Then $f$ is continuous,
> hence Riemann integrable, and $\int_{-1}^1|x|\,dx=1$. The nodes are $x_r=-1+2r/n$, and $0$ is a
> node only if $n=2r$ for some integer $r$, i.e. only if $n$ is even; so for odd $n$ the point $0$
> lies in the interior of the middle subinterval $[-1/n,\,1/n]$, and $f$ is affine on every other
> subinterval. The trapezium rule is exact on each subinterval where $f$ is affine, while on the
> middle one
> $$\frac h2\big(f(-\tfrac1n)+f(\tfrac1n)\big)=\frac1n\cdot\frac2n=\frac2{n^2},
> \qquad \int_{-1/n}^{1/n}|x|\,dx=\frac1{n^2}.$$
> Hence $T_n-\int_{-1}^1 f=\frac1{n^2}\ne0$ for every odd $n$ (e.g. $T_1=2$, error $1$). On the other hand $f'(x)=\operatorname{sgn}(x)$
> is locally constant on $[-1,1]\setminus\{0\}$, so $f''(x)=0$ at every $x\ne0$ where $f''$ is
> defined, while $f''(0)$ does not exist (indeed $f'(0)$ does not exist). Thus
> $\frac{(b-a)^3f''(\xi)}{12n^2}=\frac{2f''(\xi)}{3n^2}=0$ for every admissible $\xi\in[-1,1]$,
> and no $\xi$ whatsoever represents the error. The same conclusion holds under the opposite sign
> convention, the error being $-1/n^2\neq 0$.

The tacit, standard hypothesis — the weakest one under which the formula even makes sense — is
that $f$ be **twice differentiable** on $[a,b]$. We prove the theorem under exactly that
hypothesis. It implies the stated one: a twice differentiable function is continuous, hence
Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$. (The usual textbook hypothesis $f\in C^2[a,b]$ is a special case.)

### 0.2 Sign convention

We take *error* $=$ *approximation* $-$ *exact value*, i.e. $E_n:=T_n-\int_a^bf$. This is the
convention under which the error is $+\frac{(b-a)^3f''(\xi)}{12n^2}$, as stated. Under the
opposite convention the identical argument gives
$\int_a^bf-T_n=-\frac{(b-a)^3f''(\xi)}{12n^2}$. In both cases the magnitude of the error is
$\frac{(b-a)^3\,|f''(\xi)|}{12n^2}$, which is what "the error can be quantified as" asserts.
(That the sign is $+$ for $E_n$ is consistent with the elementary fact that for a convex $f$ the
chords lie above the graph, so the trapezium rule overestimates: $f''\ge0\Rightarrow E_n\ge0$.)

### 0.3 Theorem

> **Theorem (Trapezium rule, error term).** Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be twice differentiable on
> $[a,b]$ (the derivatives at $a$ and $b$ being one-sided). With $h,\ x_r,\ T_n$ as above there
> exists $\xi\in(a,b)$ such that
> $$\frac h2\Big(f(x_0)+f(x_n)+2\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}f(x_r)\Big)-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
> \;=\;\frac{(b-a)^3\,f''(\xi)}{12\,n^2}.$$
> In particular $\xi\in[a,b]$, as claimed.

## 1. Preliminaries

**(1a) The nodes.** The hypothesis on the normal subdivision is $x_0=a$ and
$x_r-x_{r-1}=h=\frac{b-a}{n}$ for $r=1,\dots,n$. By induction $x_r=a+rh$, and
$x_n=a+nh=a+(b-a)=b$. Since $h>0$ we have $a=x_0<x_1<\dots<x_n=b$.

**(1b) Integrability and additivity.** Differentiability of $f$ on $[a,b]$ implies continuity of
$f$ on $[a,b]$; hence $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$ and on each $[x_{r-1},x_r]$, and by
additivity of the integral over adjacent intervals,
$$\int_a^b f=\sum_{r=1}^n\int_{x_{r-1}}^{x_r}f. \tag{1}$$

**(1c) Restrictions.** If $I\subseteq[a,b]$ is a closed subinterval and $g:=f|_I$, then $g$ is
twice differentiable on $I$ with $g'=f'|_I$ and $g''=f''|_I$. Indeed, at a point $y$ interior to
$[a,b]$ but an endpoint of $I$, the two-sided derivative $f'(y)$ exists, so the corresponding
one-sided derivative of $g$ at $y$ exists and equals $f'(y)$; the same argument applied to $f'$
gives $g''(y)=f''(y)$. At points interior to $I$ nothing changes. Consequently Lemma A below may
be applied to $f$ on each $[x_{r-1},x_r]$, and Lemma B to $f'$ on any $[u,v]\subseteq[a,b]$.

**(1d) Regrouping the trapezium sum.** Each interior node $x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}$ belongs to exactly
two of the intervals $[x_{r-1},x_r]$, while $x_0$ and $x_n$ belong to one each:
$$\sum_{r=1}^n\big(f(x_{r-1})+f(x_r)\big)=\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}f(x_r)+\sum_{r=1}^{n}f(x_r)
=f(x_0)+f(x_n)+2\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}f(x_r),$$
so that
$$\sum_{r=1}^n\frac h2\big(f(x_{r-1})+f(x_r)\big)=T_n. \tag{2}$$
(For $n=1$ the empty sum is $0$ and this reads $\frac h2(f(x_0)+f(x_1))=T_1$.)

## 2. Lemma A: the error on a single subinterval

> **Lemma A.** Let $\alpha<\beta$, put $h=\beta-\alpha$, and let $g:[\alpha,\beta]\to\mathbb R$ be
> twice differentiable on $[\alpha,\beta]$ (one-sided at the endpoints). Then there exists
> $\eta\in(\alpha,\beta)$ with
> $$\frac h2\big(g(\alpha)+g(\beta)\big)-\int_\alpha^\beta g(x)\,dx=\frac{h^3}{12}\,g''(\eta).$$

*Proof.* Since $g$ is continuous on $[\alpha,\beta]$ it is Riemann integrable there. Set
$$E:=\frac h2\big(g(\alpha)+g(\beta)\big)-\int_\alpha^\beta g(x)\,dx,\qquad K:=\frac{E}{h^3},$$
which is legitimate because $h>0$. Define $\varphi:[0,h]\to\mathbb R$ by
$$\varphi(t)=\frac t2\big(g(\alpha)+g(\alpha+t)\big)-\int_\alpha^{\alpha+t}g(x)\,dx-Kt^3 .$$

*Step 1: $\varphi$ is twice differentiable on $[0,h]$.* Let $H(y)=\int_\alpha^y g(x)\,dx$ for
$y\in[\alpha,\beta]$. As $g$ is continuous, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus gives $H$
differentiable on $[\alpha,\beta]$ with $H'(y)=g(y)$ (one-sided at $\alpha,\beta$). The map
$t\mapsto\alpha+t$ is differentiable with derivative $1$ and maps $[0,h]$ onto $[\alpha,\beta]$,
so by the chain rule $t\mapsto H(\alpha+t)$ is differentiable on $[0,h]$ with derivative
$g(\alpha+t)$. Likewise $t\mapsto g(\alpha+t)$ and $t\mapsto g'(\alpha+t)$ are differentiable on
$[0,h]$ with derivatives $g'(\alpha+t)$ and $g''(\alpha+t)$. Hence, by the product and sum rules,
$\varphi$ is differentiable on $[0,h]$ with
$$\varphi'(t)=\tfrac12\big(g(\alpha)+g(\alpha+t)\big)+\tfrac t2\,g'(\alpha+t)-g(\alpha+t)-3Kt^2
=\tfrac12\big(g(\alpha)-g(\alpha+t)\big)+\tfrac t2\,g'(\alpha+t)-3Kt^2,$$
and $\varphi'$ is in turn differentiable on $[0,h]$ with
$$\varphi''(t)=-\tfrac12 g'(\alpha+t)+\tfrac12 g'(\alpha+t)+\tfrac t2\,g''(\alpha+t)-6Kt
=t\left(\tfrac12 g''(\alpha+t)-6K\right). \tag{3}$$

*Step 2: two applications of Rolle's theorem.* We have
$$\varphi(0)=0-\int_\alpha^\alpha g-0=0,\qquad
\varphi(h)=\frac h2\big(g(\alpha)+g(\beta)\big)-\int_\alpha^\beta g-Kh^3=E-E=0 .$$
$\varphi$ is continuous on $[0,h]$ (being differentiable) and differentiable on $(0,h)$, so
Rolle's theorem yields $t_1\in(0,h)$ with $\varphi'(t_1)=0$. Moreover, directly from the formula
for $\varphi'$, $\varphi'(0)=\frac12(g(\alpha)-g(\alpha))+0-0=0$. Now $\varphi'$ is continuous on
$[0,t_1]$ and differentiable on $(0,t_1)$ (by Step 1), and $\varphi'(0)=\varphi'(t_1)=0$ with
$0<t_1$; Rolle's theorem yields $t_2\in(0,t_1)$ with $\varphi''(t_2)=0$.

*Step 3: conclusion.* By $(3)$, $t_2\big(\tfrac12g''(\alpha+t_2)-6K\big)=0$, and $t_2>0$, so
$K=\tfrac1{12}g''(\alpha+t_2)$. Put $\eta:=\alpha+t_2$; then $0<t_2<t_1<h$ gives
$\eta\in(\alpha,\beta)$, and $E=Kh^3=\frac{h^3}{12}g''(\eta)$. $\blacksquare$

*Sanity check.* $g(x)=x^2$ on $[0,1]$: $E=\frac12(0+1)-\frac13=\frac16$ and
$\frac{h^3}{12}g''=\frac1{12}\cdot2=\frac16$. ✓

## 3. Lemma B (Darboux) and Lemma C (averaging values of $f''$)

> **Lemma B (Darboux's theorem).** Let $F$ be differentiable on $[u,v]$ with $u<v$ (one-sided
> derivatives at $u,v$), and let $c$ lie strictly between $F'(u)$ and $F'(v)$. Then there exists
> $\xi\in(u,v)$ with $F'(\xi)=c$.

*Proof.* Replacing $F$ by $-F$ and $c$ by $-c$ if necessary, assume $F'(u)<c<F'(v)$. Put
$G(x)=F(x)-cx$, so $G$ is differentiable on $[u,v]$ with $G'=F'-c$; being differentiable, $G$ is
continuous on the compact interval $[u,v]$ and therefore attains a minimum at some $\xi\in[u,v]$.

Since the right-hand derivative $G'(u)=F'(u)-c<0$, we have
$\lim_{x\to u^+}\frac{G(x)-G(u)}{x-u}<0$, so there is $x\in(u,v)$ with $\frac{G(x)-G(u)}{x-u}<0$,
whence $G(x)<G(u)$; therefore the minimum is not attained at $u$, i.e. $\xi\ne u$. Since the
left-hand derivative $G'(v)=F'(v)-c>0$, we have $\lim_{x\to v^-}\frac{G(v)-G(x)}{v-x}>0$, so there
is $x\in(u,v)$ with $G(v)-G(x)>0$, i.e. $G(x)<G(v)$; therefore $\xi\ne v$.

Thus $\xi\in(u,v)$ is an interior minimum of the differentiable function $G$, so by Fermat's
theorem $G'(\xi)=0$, i.e. $F'(\xi)=c$. $\blacksquare$

> **Lemma C.** Let $f$ be twice differentiable on $[a,b]$ and let $\eta_1,\dots,\eta_n\in[a,b]$.
> Then there exists $\xi$ in the closed interval $\big[\min_r\eta_r,\ \max_r\eta_r\big]$ such that
> $$\frac1n\sum_{r=1}^n f''(\eta_r)=f''(\xi).$$

*Proof.* Let $A=\frac1n\sum_{r=1}^n f''(\eta_r)$. The finite set $\{f''(\eta_r)\}$ has a least
element $m=f''(\eta_p)$ and a greatest element $M=f''(\eta_q)$ for some indices $p,q$. Since $A$
is an average of numbers lying in $[m,M]$, we have $m\le A\le M$.

If $A=m$, take $\xi=\eta_p$; if $A=M$, take $\xi=\eta_q$; in both cases $\xi\in\{\eta_1,\dots,\eta_n\}$
lies in the required interval. Otherwise $m<A<M$, so in particular $m\ne M$ and hence
$\eta_p\ne\eta_q$. Put $u=\min(\eta_p,\eta_q)$ and $v=\max(\eta_p,\eta_q)$, so $u<v$ and
$[u,v]\subseteq[\min_r\eta_r,\max_r\eta_r]\subseteq[a,b]$. By (1c), $F:=f'|_{[u,v]}$ is
differentiable on $[u,v]$ with $F'=f''|_{[u,v]}$, and $\{F'(u),F'(v)\}=\{m,M\}$, so $A$ lies
strictly between $F'(u)$ and $F'(v)$. Lemma B provides $\xi\in(u,v)$ with $f''(\xi)=F'(\xi)=A$.
$\blacksquare$

(If one assumes the stronger hypothesis $f\in C^2[a,b]$, Lemma B is unnecessary: $f''$ is then
continuous and the ordinary Intermediate Value Theorem applies on $[u,v]$.)

## 4. Proof of the Theorem

By $(1)$ and $(2)$,
$$T_n-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
=\sum_{r=1}^n\left[\frac h2\big(f(x_{r-1})+f(x_r)\big)-\int_{x_{r-1}}^{x_r}f(x)\,dx\right]. \tag{4}$$

Fix $r\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. By (1c) the restriction of $f$ to $[x_{r-1},x_r]$ is twice differentiable
there, with second derivative $f''$, and $x_r-x_{r-1}=h>0$. Lemma A therefore provides
$\eta_r\in(x_{r-1},x_r)$ with
$$\frac h2\big(f(x_{r-1})+f(x_r)\big)-\int_{x_{r-1}}^{x_r}f(x)\,dx=\frac{h^3}{12}f''(\eta_r).$$
Substituting into $(4)$,
$$T_n-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\frac{h^3}{12}\sum_{r=1}^n f''(\eta_r)
=\frac{n\,h^3}{12}\cdot\frac1n\sum_{r=1}^n f''(\eta_r). \tag{5}$$

By Lemma C there is $\xi\in[\min_r\eta_r,\max_r\eta_r]$ with
$\frac1n\sum_{r=1}^n f''(\eta_r)=f''(\xi)$. Since $\eta_r\in(x_{r-1},x_r)\subseteq(a,b)$ for every
$r$, both $\min_r\eta_r$ and $\max_r\eta_r$ lie in $(a,b)$, hence
$[\min_r\eta_r,\max_r\eta_r]\subseteq(a,b)$ and so $\xi\in(a,b)\subset[a,b]$.

Finally,
$$n\,h^3=n\left(\frac{b-a}{n}\right)^3=\frac{(b-a)^3}{n^2},$$
so $(5)$ becomes
$$\frac h2\Big(f(x_0)+f(x_n)+2\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}f(x_r)\Big)-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
=\frac{(b-a)^3\,f''(\xi)}{12\,n^2},\qquad \xi\in(a,b).$$
$\blacksquare$

## 5. Remarks

1. **Error bound.** If in addition $f''$ is bounded on $[a,b]$, say $|f''|\le M_2$ (automatic when
 $f\in C^2[a,b]$, by the Extreme Value Theorem), then
 $$\left|T_n-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\right|\le\frac{(b-a)^3M_2}{12\,n^2}=O\!\left(\frac1{n^2}\right),$$
 so the trapezium rule converges to $\int_a^bf$ at second order in $h=(b-a)/n$.
2. **Sign.** If $f$ is convex on $[a,b]$ (equivalently, $f''\ge0$ there), the theorem gives
 $T_n\ge\int_a^bf$: the trapezium rule overestimates. Reversed for concave $f$.
3. **Sharpness of the constant.** For $f(x)=x^2$ we have $f''\equiv2$ and the theorem gives
 $T_n-\int_a^bf=\frac{(b-a)^3}{6n^2}$ exactly, so the constant $\frac1{12}$ cannot be improved.
4. **Exactness on affine functions.** If $f(x)=px+q$ then $f''\equiv0$ and the error vanishes, as
 it must, since the chords coincide with the graph.
